title.en: The Coming of the Tuatha Dé Danann from the Four Cities
title.zh: 圖阿哈·迪·丹安自四城乘霧而來

region.zh: 愛爾蘭康諾特馬格尼亞平原（象徵定位）

texts.period: Recorded in Lebor Gabála Érenn and Cath Maige Tuired traditions, 11th-12th c. manuscripts; Lady Gregory retelling 1904

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book One, Chapter I, eBook #14465

summary.en: The people of the goddess Dana arrive in Ireland from four cities of learning in the north, bearing four treasures — the Stone of Destiny, the sword, the spear of victory and the ever-satisfying cauldron — and come down through the air and the high air in a mist on Beltaine morning, the Firbolgs who hold the island seeing nothing but fog on the hills.
summary.zh: 達娜女神之民自北方四座學藝之城而來，攜四寶——命運之石、劍、勝利之矛、永不空乏之釜——於五月朔日乘霧自空中降臨愛爾蘭；先居之巴格斯人（Bag Men）惟見山間白霧，不見其人。

sensitivity.note: Symbolic pin: the mist-landing site is unlocatable in the narrative; Magh Nia in Connacht is where the Tuatha settled before the First Battle. Living Irish-language and Gaelic communities hold the tradition of the Sídhe; stories are collected from public-domain print, not field consultation.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Gods and Fighting Men, Book One ch. 1: It was in a mist the Tuatha Dé Danann, the people of the gods of Dana, came through the air and the high air to Ireland. They came from the north, from four cities where they fought their battle for learning — Falias, Gorias, Finias and Murias — taught by four wise men, and they carried from those cities their four treasures: the Lia Fáil, the Stone of Destiny, from Falias; a sword from Gorias; a spear of victory from Finias; and from Murias the cauldron no company ever went away from unsatisfied. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book One ch. 1; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Nuada was their king; among the chief men were Ogma who taught writing, Diancecht the healer, Neit god of battle, Credenus the craftsman and Goibniu the smith. Among the women were the battle goddesses Badb and Macha, the Morrígu the Crow of Battle, Eire and Fodla and Banba who gave their names to Ireland, Eadon nurse of poets, and Brigit of poetry and healing, whose face was one side ugly and one side comely. The three things they set above all others were the plough, the sun and the hazel tree. They had a well below the sea where nine hazels of wisdom dropped their blossoms into purple water and five salmon ate the nuts; whoever ate one salmon would know all wisdom and all poetry. They landed on Beltaine, May Day, and the Firbolgs saw only a mist lying on the hills. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book One ch. 1; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men, London 1904 (public domain); underlying sources: Cath Maige Tuired (Stokes, Irische Texte, 1891); Lebor Gabála Érenn (Macalister edition 1938-56, copyright)

narrative.en:
The arrival of the Tuatha Dé Danann is Ireland's true myth of creation — not a making of the world out of chaos, but a consecration of an island by a people who are gods, poets, smiths and healers at once.

They did not come by land or sea. The early tales insist it was in a mist, through the air and the high air, from the north. Behind them lay four cities of the far north — Falias the great, Gorias the shining, Finias and Murias the rich — where the young gods had fought their battle for learning, the meaning being that knowledge itself was won like a war. In each city sat one wise teacher: Senias in Murias, Arias the fair-haired poet in Finias, Urias of the noble nature in Gorias, and Morias in Falias. From those cities the newcomers brought four treasures that map their whole theology: from Falias the Lia Fáil, the Stone of Destiny that would cry out under the feet of a lawful king; from Gorias the Sword; from Finias the Spear of Victory; and from Murias the Cauldron that no company ever went away from unsatisfied. Stone, blade, point and vessel — sovereignty, war, victory and abundance.

Nuada was their king. Ogma his brother taught them writing. Diancecht understood healing, Neit was a god of battle, Credenus the craftsman and Goibniu the smith, whose spear-points never missed and whose ale kept age and death away. Among their women were the battle-goddesses Badb, Macha and the Morrígu the Crow of Battle; Eire, Fodla and Banba, three daughters of the Dagda who would each give her name to Ireland; Eadon, nurse of poets; and Brigit — woman of poetry, healing and smith's work, inventor of the whistle for calling through the night — whose one face was ugly and the other beautiful, whose name meant a fiery arrow. Dana herself, the mother of the gods, was beyond them all.

The three things they put above all others were the plough, the sun and the hazel tree — Coll the hazel, Cecht the plough, Grian the sun, in whose three names Ireland was said to be divided. Below the sea lay their well of wisdom, where nine hazels grew and rained their blossoms into purple water; five salmon waiting there ate the falling nuts, and the red spots on their skin carried the color of that knowledge. Whoever ate one of those salmon would know all wisdom and all poetry. Seven streams of inspiration rose from that well and turned back into it again, and all people of many arts have drunk from them — the same well that Cormac would later see at the heart of Manannan's otherworld.

They landed on the first day of Beltaine, May Day, on the northwest coast of Connacht. The Firbolgs who held the island — the Men of the Bag, come earlier from the south — saw nothing at all: a mist lying on the hills. But their king Eochaid son of Erc dreamed a dream, and his druids read it: a strong enemy was coming. The myth thus begins as the old world's nightmare, and the new people of the arts walking out of fog to take the island that the three queens of Ireland, Eire and Fodla and Banba, would make for their own names.
narrative.zh: 圖阿哈·迪·丹安（達娜女神之民）之降臨，乃愛爾蘭真正的創世神話：非由混沌造世界，而是以神與匠師之民將島嶼祝聖。其眾不履陸海，乘霧自北方高空而來；北方四城——大法利亞斯、光戈里亞斯、菲尼亞斯、富繆里亞斯——為學藝而戰之地，四賢者各授其藝。攜四寶而來：法利亞斯之命運之石（Lia Fáil，合法国王踐之則鳴）、戈里亞斯之劍、菲尼亞斯之勝利之矛、繆里亞斯永不使賓客空乏之釜——即主權、戰爭、勝利與豐足之總圖。努阿達為王；歐格瑪授文字，迪安徹特司療，內特司戰，克雷德努斯司工藝，戈伊布尼烏司鍛冶——其矛無虛發，其麥酒令人不老不死。女神輩有戰神巴德布、瑪哈與戰烏摩里古；達格達三女艾雷、福德拉與班巴後各以名予愛爾蘭；詩人之乳母伊頓；與兼詩、療、鍛冶之布里吉特——一面醜一面美，名義為「火之箭」。達娜母神居眾之上。其所最尊者三：犁、日、榛。海底有智慧之泉，九株榛樹落花於紫水；五鮭食堅果，食之者得全知與全詩。至五月朔日（Beltaine）登岸於康諾特西北，巴格斯人惟見山間之霧。其王伊奧凱得夢，德魯伊釋之：強敵將至。神話遂以舊世之噩夢始，以新藝之民自霧中走出、島將以三女神之名命名終。

functions: Creation-by-consecration: the island is claimed by a god-race through arts and treasures, not by chaos-splitting
Charter of the four pagan mysteries — stone (sovereignty), sword, spear, cauldron — later mirrored in the four Treasures of the Sídhe
Aition of Beltaine: the gods land at the fire-feast of May Day
Etiology of Ireland's names through the three queens Eire, Fodla, Banba

title.en: The First Battle of Mag Tuired: Tuath Dé against Fir Bolg
title.zh: 第一次馬格·圖雷德之戰：達娜之民對巴格斯人

region.zh: 愛爾蘭馬優郡馬格·圖雷德平原（康鎮）

texts.period: Recorded in Cath Maige Tuired Cunga traditions and Lebor Gabála; 11th c. manuscripts; Gregory retelling 1904

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book One, Chapter I, eBook #14465

summary.en: The Firbolg champion Sreng and the god-champion Bres meet half-way over their shields and trade spears as proof of one another's peoples; parley fails, and in the first battle on Magh Tuired the gods win, their king Nuada losing his arm, while the defeated Firbolgs are given Connacht to keep.
summary.zh: 巴格斯勇士斯倫格與神族勇士布雷斯隔盾相望、互換長矛以驗其族；談判既破，馬格·圖雷德首戰之中神族雖勝而王努阿達失臂，敗者巴格斯人獲賜康諾特以居。

sensitivity.note: Location verified: the First Battle is traditionally placed at Mag Tuired near Cong, Co. Mayo. The Firbolgs survive in the tale as ancestors of later heroes (Ferdiad, Erc).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Sreng son of Erc came out from Teamhair with his strong red-brown shield and two thick-handled spears to look at the strangers; Bres came from the Tuatha Dé to meet him. Each thrust his shield into the ground and looked over the rim; each was in dread of the other's spear — the thin sharp darts of the gods, the heavy blunt Craisech of the Firbolgs whose thrust was death or wounds that never healed. They exchanged spears so each host could see what the other was used to, and Bres brought back his offer: give us half of Ireland in peace, or there will be battle. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book One ch. 1; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: The Firbolgs would not yield the half, saying the strangers would soon take the whole. The queens Badb, Macha and the Morrígu covered the Firbolgs' ground with mists, clouds of darkness, showers of fire and blood for three days until the three druids of the Firbolgs broke the enchantment. The battle began on Midsummer day: three nines of hurlers on each side were all killed, the hosts fought four days, the physicians of each side bathed the living in healing herbs each evening. On the fourth day the gods prevailed; King Eochaid, thirst-driven off the field, was overtaken and slain at the strand of Traigh Eothaile, and Sreng was left with the last three hundred of eleven battalions. Nuada offered peace: Sreng chose Connacht, and his people lived there after — of them came Ferdiad, who fought Cuchulainn at the ford, and Erc, who gave him his death. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book One ch. 1; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men, London 1904 (public domain); cf. Cath Maige Tuired Cunga in later dindsenchas (Gwynn, Metrical Dindsenchas, copyright)

narrative.en:
Before the gods could be kings of Ireland they had to win it from men — and the tale of the First Battle of Mag Tuired is told not as a slaughter but as a meeting of two armies who discover they are kin.

The Firbolgs, the Men of the Bag, held the island. When word came to their king Eochaid son of Erc at Teamhair that a new race had settled at Magh Rein — whether from the earth, the skies or the wind nobody could say — there was no great wonder on him, for he had dreamed, and his druids had read the dream: a strong enemy was coming. He sent Sreng, a great fighting man, out toward the strangers; and the Tuatha Dé sent Bres to meet him. The two champions walked one toward the other slowly, shields raised, each stopping at talking distance — and then each put his shield before his body and struck it hard into the ground, and looked at one another over the rim.

The first discovery was that they spoke the same tongue: when Sreng heard Irish on Bres's lips he was less uneasy, and they drew near and asked after one another's kindred. The second discovery was mutual respect for weapons. Sreng feared the thin, sharp, hard-pointed spears of the gods; Bres feared the thick-handled Craisech of the Firbolgs, blunt at the side, that broke shields and crushed flesh and bone, whose thrust was death or a wound that never healed. So they exchanged spears, so that the fighters on each side might see what the other was used to — a courteous detail that marks this as a tale told by both peoples' descendants. Bres delivered the offer: half of Ireland in peace, or battle. Sreng advised his king to share the country; Eochaid and his chief men refused: 'if we give the half they will soon take the whole.'

Then the gods showed their other weapons. Three queens — Badb, Macha and the Morrígu — went to Teamhair and by enchantment brought mists, clouds of darkness, showers of fire and of blood over the Firbolgs for three days, until three Firbolg druids, Cesarn, Gnathach and Ingnathach, broke the spell: druid against druid before spear against spear.

The battle itself was contracted like a lawful duel. The gods' hurlers went out first and were killed to a man; Eochaid asked whether the battle would be every day or every second day; Nuada answered every day, but with equal numbers on each side — and Eochaid agreed unhappily, for the Firbolgs were the more numerous. For four days the hosts fought, and each evening the physicians of both sides made a bath of healing herbs so the maimed could rise sound for the next day's fight. On the fourth day the gods got the upper hand. A great thirst came on Eochaid; he went off the field for drink with three fifties protecting him, was pursued to the strand of Traigh Eothaile, and fell there, and a great heap of stones was raised over his grave.

When only three hundred of the eleven battalions were left, and Sreng at their head, Nuada offered peace and a province of their choosing. Sreng took Connacht, and the Firbolgs lived there and their children after them — of whom, the tale insists, came Ferdiad, who held the ford against Cuchulainn, and Erc, who gave Cuchulainn his death. The conquered are not erased but saved for the heroic age to come: an epic's cast of enemies being its oldest friends.
narrative.zh: 神欲為愛爾蘭之王，必先自人族手中得之；首戰之記非屠殺而為兩族相認之會。巴格斯人（Fir Bolg）先居其島。新族至馬格·雷因消息傳至塔拉王伊奧凱時，王無大異——因已得夢兆，德魯伊釋曰強敵將至。王遣勇士斯倫格窺敵，神族遣布雷斯相迎。二勇士緩行相向，各持盾、至語距而止，插盾於地、隔盾沿相望。第一發現乃同語：斯倫格聞布雷斯操愛爾蘭語而稍安。第二發現乃互敬其兵器：神族畏其厚重鈍邊之Craisech矛（可破盾碎骨，其創不愈），巴格斯人畏其尖銳細矛。遂互換長矛，使兩軍各見敵之慣技。布雷斯獻議：半島和平相讓，否則一戰。斯倫格勸王分土；伊奧凱拒之：『予其半，彼將取其全。』三女神巴德布、瑪哈、摩里古以咒布霧、黑雲、火雨血雨三日，直至巴格斯三德魯伊破其咒。戰如合法決鬥：神族擲球手先出而盡歿；每日一戰，兩軍人數相等，醫者夜以草藥浴傷者使明日復戰；第四日神族得勢，伊奧凱渴而出戰場就飲，為追兵及於特拉伊·埃奧泰爾海灘，死焉，冢上壘巨石。十一營餘三百人，斯倫格為首；努阿達許和，擇省而居——得康諾特。其子孫後出弗迪亞（於渡口力拒庫丘林）與埃爾克（終致庫丘林之死）：敗者不滅，而留待英雄時代。

functions: Charter of conquest-by-law: the battle is contracted (equal numbers, rest days) as a lawful duel, modeling诉讼 of sovereignty transfer
Etiology of Connacht's population: Fir Bolg survival as ancestors of later Ulster-Cycle heroes
Dual-inheritance epic logic: the conquered remain as the epic's future enemies and friends
Druid weather-magic narrative: battle begins in the heavens before it begins on the field

title.en: Nuada Loses the Kingship and Gains a Silver Hand

region.en: Teamhair (Hill of Tara), Co. Meath, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭米斯郡塔拉王丘

texts.period: Recorded in Cath Maige Tuired traditions, 11th c.; Gregory retelling 1904

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book One, Chapter II, eBook #14465

summary.en: Nuada, wounded by Sreng in the First Battle, is deposed because a law of the Tuatha Dé forbids any king not perfect in shape; Diancecht the physician makes him a silver arm with movement in every finger, and when the king is healed Nuada is restored — but his son Miach, who restores the arm of flesh, is killed by his own father's thrown sword.
summary.zh: 努阿達於首戰為斯倫格所傷失臂，因神族之法『形不全者不得為王』而被廢；醫神迪安徹特製銀臂、指指能動；及其復原，努阿達復位——然其子米亞克以真臂復接者，竟為其父擲劍所殺。

sensitivity.note: The perfect-body kingship law (no blemished king) is a documented legal-theological motif of Irish kingship tales; translated from public-domain print.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Nuada had won the battle but lost his own arm, struck off by Sreng; and by that loss troubles came on his people, for it was a law with the Tuatha Dé Danann that no man that was not perfect in shape should be king. So he was put out of the kingship, and Bres, the most beautiful of their young men, was chosen in his place. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book One ch. 2; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Diancecht the healer made an arm of silver for Nuada, with movement in every finger, and from that he was called Nuada Argat-lámh, of the Silver Hand. But Miach, son of Diancecht, took the king's own hand that had been struck off, set it in its place saying 'Joint to joint, and sinew to sinew,' and for three days and three nights healed it — the first day against his side, the second against his breast, the third with blackened bulrushes — till the king was whole. Diancecht, vexed that his son did a better cure than himself, threw his sword at Miach's head: the first blow cut flesh and was healed, the second reached bone and was healed, the third and fourth cut out the brain, and Miach died. Three hundred and sixty-five herbs grew from his grave; his sister Airmed laid them out on her cloak by their virtue, but Diancecht mixed them up, so that no one knows all their powers to this day. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book One ch. 2; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men, London 1904 (public domain); underlying: Cath Maige Tuired (Stokes, Irische Texte 1891)

narrative.en:
Nuada's wound is the hinge on which the whole coming of Lugh turns: from a lost arm flow a deposition, a bad reign, a satire, and eventually the war for Ireland itself.

In the First Battle Sreng's Craisech had sheared off the god-king's arm. Victory was not enough to keep him his throne, for it was a law with the Tuatha Dé Danann that no man who was not perfect in shape should be king — bodily integrity and sovereignty were one thing. The assembly chose Bres in his place, the most beautiful of their young men, so comely that any beautiful thing — a plain, a dun, ale, a flame, a woman, a horse — would be praised as 'beautiful as Bres'. Whose son he was only his mother knew.

While Bres reigned badly, Diancecht the physician made his king a new arm of silver, with movement in every finger, and Nuada was called Argat-lámh, of the Silver Hand, for ever after. The tale then records the strangest of its cures: Miach, the physician's own son and a better healer than his father, met a young man at Teamhair who had lost an eye and asked for another; Miach set in its place the eye of a cat in the man's lap — which worked, after a fashion, waking when the man wanted to sleep and sleeping when he wanted to watch an army. Not satisfied with the silver prosthesis, Miach took Nuada's severed hand and set it on the stump saying 'joint to joint, and sinew to sinew': three days and three nights he worked, the first day holding the hand against the king's side, the second against his breast until it was covered with skin, the third laying on blackened bulrushes, and the king was healed.

Then comes the tale's dark final turn. Diancecht, vexed that his son did a better cure than himself, threw his sword at Miach's head. The first blow cut the flesh, and the lad healed it with his own skill; the second reached the bone and was cured; the third and fourth cut out the brain, which no physician could cure, and Miach died. Herbs sprang from his grave, three hundred and sixty-five of them, one for every joint and sinew; his sister Airmed spread them on her cloak and sorted them by their virtues — and Diancecht, seeing it, came and mixed them together, so that no one knows all their right powers to this day: an aition for why healing is a craft of search, not of certainty.

With the king whole in body, the Tuatha gathered at Teamhair and bade Bres give up the kingship he had held long enough, though not willingly. Nuada was restored. Bres, in his vexation, went to his mother Eri to learn his race — and learned that his father was Elatha, king of the Fomor, who had come over a level sea in a silver vessel with gold-sewn clothes and five rings of gold about his neck. From that discovery comes the alliance that brings Balor and the great invasion. The proverb the tale teaches is Bres's own father's: their good-will would be better than their curses — prosperity of the people over majesty of the king.
narrative.zh: 努阿達之失臂，乃魯格降世之樞紐：一臂之失，牽出廢立、暴政、諷刺詩，乃至為愛爾蘭而戰。首戰中斯倫格之Craisech矛斷神王之臂；然勝利不足以保其位，因神族之法：形不全者不得為王——身體完整與主權合而為一。眾遂立布雷斯，其美冠絕一時，凡美物皆以『美如布雷斯』譽之。暴政期間，醫神迪安徹特為王製銀臂，指指能動，努阿達自此稱『銀手』。故事續記奇療：其子米亞克醫術勝父，為獨眼青年置貓目；又不滿銀臂之假，取王斷臂接於殘端，誦曰『節對節、筋對筋』，三日三夜之功——首日貼脅、次日貼胸至膚生、三日敷火燻之黑藺草——王乃復原。而後故事轉暗：迪安徹特嫉子勝己，擲劍擊其首；一擊破膚、子自愈之，二擊及骨、亦愈之，三四擊碎腦，無醫可救，米亞克遂死。墓上生三百六十五種草藥，其妹艾爾梅德以衣攤列、按效分類；迪安徹特見而攪亂之，故世人不盡知諸藥之性——此為『療術乃搜尋之藝而非確然之術』之釋義。王既體全，眾會於塔拉，令布雷斯讓位（彼不甚願），努阿達復位。布雷斯怨憤，往問母親世系——得知其父乃弗摩爾王埃拉塔：乘銀舟、衣金線服、頸戴五金環、渡如鏡之海而來者。由此發現生出引巴羅大軍入侵之盟。故事之諺語即其父之言：『民之善願勝於民之詛咒』——民之繁榮重於王之威嚴。

title.en: The Reign of Bres and the First Satire of Ireland
title.zh: 布雷斯之治與愛爾蘭首篇諷刺詩

region.en: Teamhair (Hill of Tara), Co. Meath, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭米斯郡塔拉王丘

texts.period: Recorded in Cath Maige Tuired and Lebor Gabála traditions, 11th-12th c.; Gregory retelling 1904

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book One, Chapter II, eBook #14465

summary.en: Bres the beautiful king taxes his own gods into servitude — Ogma gathering firewood, the Dagda digging raths and fed on by a blind parasite — until the poet Corpre, lodged in a dark cell and given three dry cakes, pronounces against him the first satire ever made in Ireland, and from that day there is no good luck with Bres.
summary.zh: 美王布雷斯橫徵暴斂，使其族之神為僕——歐格瑪拾薪、達格達掘塹且遭盲蟲剝食——直至詩人科爾普雷被安置暗室、僅得三塊乾餅，遂對王吟出愛爾蘭首篇諷刺詩；自此布雷斯厄運纏身。

sensitivity.note: The satire (áer) as an instrument that destroys a king is a documented feature of Irish kingship ideology; retold from public-domain print.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: In spite of Bres being so beautiful, his reign brought no good luck to his people, for the Fomor put tribute on them — a third of their corn, a third of their milk, a third of their children — so that there was not smoke rising from a roof in Ireland that was not under tribute. Bres himself taxed every house for the milk of hornless dun cows; Nechtan, by the druid Findgoll's advice, singed all the cows of Ireland brown in a fire of fern to deceive him, and another time they made three hundred wooden cows with pails of bog-stuff, which Bres drank thinking it milk. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book One ch. 2; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Ogma the shining poet was set to carry firing to the palace, so weak with hunger that the sea swept away two-thirds of his bundle daily; the Dagda was put to dig raths, where the blind man Cridenbel exacted the three best bits of his food every night until Angus's three pieces of gold, hidden in the bits, killed the parasite. Then the poet Corpre, son of Etain, came looking for hospitality and was put in a little dark narrow house without fire, furniture or bed, and given three small dry cakes on a little dish. Going across the green in the morning he said: 'Without food ready on a dish; without milk enough for a calf to grow on; without shelter; without light in the darkness of night; without enough to pay a story-teller — may that be the prosperity of Bres.' And from that day there was no good luck with Bres; and that was the first satire ever made in Ireland. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book One ch. 2; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men, London 1904 (public domain); underlying: Cath Maige Tuired, ed. Stokes 1891

narrative.en:
Bres's reign is the mythic charter of Irish satire — the tale that tells why a poet's word can put a king down.

The trouble began with taxes. The Fomor, dwelling beyond the sea or below it westward, dreadful in aspect, maimed, under a giant and his mother, put tribute on Ireland: a third of its corn, a third of its milk, a third of its children — so that there was not smoke rising from a roof in Ireland that was not under tribute to them. And Bres made no stand against them. He taxed the gods themselves, demanding of every house the milk of hornless dun cows and cows of a single color in quantities enough for a hundred men; the Ireland of the tale cheats him twice — once when Nechtan, on the druid Findgoll's advice, singed every cow in the land brown in a fire of fern and rubbed them with flaxseed ash, and once when three hundred wooden cows were milked before him, their black bog-stuff drunk by the king himself, who was not the better of it for a long time.

The inner court was no better. In Bres's house the knives of the chiefs were never greased, no smell of ale was on their breaths, and there was no call for poets, singers, harpers, pipers, horn-blowers, jugglers or fools — hospitality itself had been abolished. Ogma the shining poet was ordered to bring fuel for the whole army every day from the islands of Mod, so weakened by hunger that the sea carried off two-thirds of each day's bundle. The Dagda was set to dig raths, and there the blind man Cridenbel with the sharp tongue fastened on him, exacting 'the three best bits' of the Dagda's share — bits the size of a good pig — until the Dagda's son Angus Og armed him with three pieces of gold to hide in the food, which turned inside Cridenbel and killed him, a death the king first misread as poisoning until the body was cut open and the gold found.

Wages were the Dagda's heifer — black and black-maned, chosen on Angus's advice, and secretly destined to matter at the war's end. Then came the poem. Corpre, son of Etain, poet of the Tuatha Dé, sought the king's house and was lodged in a little dark narrow house without fire, furniture or bed, and feasted with three small dry cakes on a little dish. Crossing the green in the morning he gave his judgment in four bitter lines: without food ready on a dish; without milk enough for a calf to grow on; without shelter; without light in the darkness of night; without enough to pay a story-teller — 'may that be the prosperity of Bres.' From that day there was no good luck with Bres, and he went down for ever after: for that was the first satire ever made in Ireland. The deposed king would learn his race from his mother Eri — a Fomorian father, Elatha, whose ring fitted no finger but Bres's own — and ride to his own people to buy back a throne with an army. But the poem had already judged the reign: sovereignty is held not by force but by feeding.
narrative.zh: 布雷斯之治乃愛爾蘭諷刺詩（áer）之神話憲章——即解釋詩人一言何以能廢君之故事。禍起於稅：弗摩爾人居海外或海西之下，形貌可怖、殘缺不全，為巨魔及其母所率，向愛爾蘭徵稅——三分之一穀、三分之一乳、三分之一孩童——致使愛爾蘭無一縷炊煙不在其貢賦之下，而布雷斯不予抵抗。彼反苛徵神族：責每戶獻無角棕牛之乳、純色牛之乳至足百人之量；愛爾蘭兩番欺之——內克坦奉德魯伊芬戈爾之策，以蕨火燻烤全境牛群使成棕色，以亞麻灰塗之；又以三百木牛、黑沼之泥充乳，王親嘗之，久而不愈。宮內亦劣：群臣之刀永不上油，無酒氣於鼻，詩人、歌者、豎琴師、笛手、號手、弄人皆無所召——款待之道廢矣。光耀詩人歐格瑪被役使自莫德群島為全軍日運柴薪，飢弱至海每日捲去其束薪三分之二。達格達被遣掘塹築堡，盲者克里登貝爾利舌索其『三塊上品』，其量如豚；安古斯·歐格以三金塊藏食中予之，金入腹而蟲死，王初疑為毒藥，剖屍見金乃明。其傭值為一黑鬃小母牛——依安古斯之言擇之，暗中註定於戰尾見功。繼而詩篇至：科爾普雷（艾塔恩之子、神族之詩人）求宿，被置暗狹之室，無火無床無几，僅以三塊乾餅為饗。晨起過草場，以四行苦句下其判：『盤中無食；無乳以哺犢；無庇護；黑夜無光；無以酬講古者——願此為布雷斯之繁榮。』自是布雷斯厄運相隨、永不復振：此即愛爾蘭首篇諷刺詩。廢王將自其母埃里得知世系——弗摩爾父埃拉塔，其戒指惟合布雷斯之指——遂返己族欲以軍隊贖回王位。然詩已斷其治：主權之持，不在力而在饗。

title.en: The Birth of Lugh in Balor's Tower of Glass
title.zh: 魯格誕生於巴羅之玻璃塔

region.en: Tory Island (Torach), Co. Donegal, Ireland — Tower of Glass (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭多尼戈爾郡托里島（象徵定位：玻璃之塔）

texts.period: Recorded in medieval Irish tradition (Book of the Dun Cow and later); Gregory retelling 1904

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book Two, Chapter I, eBook #14465

summary.en: A druid foretells that Balor of the Evil Eye will die by his own grandson; Balor shuts his daughter Ethlinn in a tower with twelve women and never lets her hear a man's name — until the Druid woman Birog disguises Cian in woman's clothes, carries him across the sea in a blast of wind, and Ethlinn bears a son who is saved from the drowning-cloth by the same enchantress.
summary.zh: 德魯伊預言巴羅將死於己孫之手；巴羅遂閉女艾斯琳於玻璃塔中，以十二女侍之，永不令其聞男子之名——直至女德魯伊比羅格將西安扮女裝、乘風渡海入塔；艾斯琳產子，溺衣之針落而子獲救。

sensitivity.note: Pin: Tory Island (Toraigh) is the traditional seat of Balor in Irish tradition and in living Tory folklore; the 'Tower of Glass' itself is otherworldly and the pin is symbolic.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: A druid foretold that it was by his own grandson Balor would get his death; he had but one child, a daughter named Ethlinn, and he shut her up in the tower on the island of glass, with twelve women to guard her, and bade them never let her see a man or hear the name of a man. She grew beautiful, and sometimes she would see men passing in currachs, and sometimes a man in her dreams; but the women gave her no answer when she spoke of it. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book Two ch. 1; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Cian of the Tuatha Dé, robbed by Balor of his wonder-cow the Glas Gaibhnenn, was told by a druid that while Balor lived no one could come within reach of his Evil Eye; so the woman-druid Birog of the Mountain dressed Cian in woman's clothes and carried him across the sea in a blast of wind to the tower, passing them in to Ethlinn as a high queen she had saved. Birog's spells put the women to sleep, and when Ethlinn saw Cian she said that was the face she had seen in her dreams. When her time came Balor bade his people throw the child into the sea-current in a cloth fastened with a pin; the pin dropped, the child slipped into the water, and was thought drowned — but Birog brought him away and gave him to Taillte, daughter of the King of the Great Plain, to foster. Thus Lugh was born and reared. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book Two ch. 1; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men, London 1904 (public domain); underlying: Oidheadh Chlainne Tuireann and related texts (Whitley Stokes editions, public domain)

narrative.en:
Lugh's birth is the Irish Zeus-and-Cronus: a prophecy of filicide answered with a tower, a disguise, and a pin that drops at the right moment.

Balor of the Strong Blows — some said of the Evil Eye — lived on the island of the Tower of Glass, dangerous for ships, which the Fomor plundered as they passed. Some remembered the sons of Nemed coming near it in the old time and attacking what looked like men on a glass tower with druid spells; the tower vanished under their assault, but a great wave rose and all their ships went down. The tower stood again as before, and Balor lived in it. His one deadly eye had been ruined innocently: passing a house where his father's druids were making spells of death, he had looked in at the open window, and the smoke of the poisonous brew went into his eye. Ever after he kept it closed, and when he wanted an enemy dead his men lifted the lid with a ring of ivory.

Then a druid foretold that by his own grandson he would get his death. Balor had one child, Ethlinn; he shut her in the tower and set twelve women over her, charged never to let her see a man or hear a man's name. She grew up beautiful, watching currachs pass below and dreaming of faces her guards would not name.

Meanwhile on the mainland Cian, brother of the smith Goibniu, kept the Glas Gaibhnenn, the cow whose milk never failed, coveted by everyone who heard of her. When Balor stole her — slipping the halter from Cian's brother's hand while disguised as a little red-haired boy who told a poisoned tale of brothers cheating — a druid told Cian the truth: while Balor lived, the cow would never be recovered, for none could come within reach of that eye. So Cian went to Birog of the Mountain. She dressed him in woman's clothes and carried him over the sea on a blast of wind, and at the tower called for shelter for 'a high queen she had saved from hardship'; the women of the tower could not refuse a woman of the Tuatha Dé. Birog's enchantments put them all to sleep, and Ethlinn, seeing Cian, said at once that was the face she had seen in her dreams. She gave him her love; he was carried away again on a wind.

When her time came, Balor had the child bound in a cloth with a pin and thrown into the sea-current. On the way across an arm of the sea the pin dropped; the child slipped from the cloth, and those who carried him thought him drowned. Birog of the Mountain had him, and gave him to Cian, who fostered him on Taillte, daughter of the King of the Great Plain. Thus Lugh was born and reared — the grandson marked for his grandfather's death, kept by an enchantress, named for the mastery of every art that would later open the gates of Teamhair.
narrative.zh: 魯格之誕生即愛爾蘭之宙斯與克羅諾斯：弒親預言，以塔、偽裝與適時落下之一針回應之。強擊者巴羅——或稱邪眼巴羅——居海上玻璃之塔，航船過者皆遭弗摩爾劫掠。傳說內梅德之子昔年曾近此塔，見塔上似人者，以德魯伊咒擊之；塔雖隱沒，巨浪捲起，其船盡沒。塔復如故，巴羅居焉。其致命之眼得之無辜：一日過其父德魯伊施死亡咒法之屋，自開窗窺視，毒咒之煙入其目。此後常閉其瞼；欲殺敵時，左右以象牙環啟之。德魯伊預言：其死必於己孫之手。巴羅唯一女艾斯琳；閉之於塔，以十二女侍之，永不令見男子、聞男子之名。女漸長而美，觀舟楫過於塔下，夢中有面而侍女不答。陸上，鍛冶神戈伊布尼烏之弟西安畜神牛格拉斯·蓋布嫩，其乳不竭，聞者皆覬覦。巴羅扮紅髮小童，以兄弟相欺之毒言騙取牛韁而奪牛；德魯伊告西安：巴羅在世一日，牛不可復，蓋無人能近邪眼之及。西安遂求山間女德魯伊比羅格。比羅格令西安著女裝、乘風渡海，至塔前以『救護之貴婦』求宿；塔中諸女不敢拒神族之女。比羅格咒眾皆眠，艾斯琳見西安即曰：此即夢中之面。遂以身相許；西安復乘風而去。產期既至，巴羅命以布裹嬰、以針別之，投諸海流。渡一海臂之際，針落，嬰滑出，眾以為溺。比羅格取之，交西安，寄養於大平原王之女泰爾特。魯格遂生而育——註定殺祖父之孫，由術士所護，日後以百藝之師啟塔拉之門。

Etiology of Tory Island folklore: Balor's seat located on the living island of Toraigh

title.en: Lugh at the Door of Teamhair: Master of All Arts
title.zh: 魯格於塔拉門前：百藝之師

region.en: Teamhair (Hill of Tara), Co. Meath, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭米斯郡塔拉王丘

texts.period: Recorded in medieval Irish prose (Samhain episode in the tale of Mag Tuired); Gregory retelling 1904

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book Two, Chapter I, eBook #14465

summary.en: At the door of Nuada's feast at Tara the doorkeepers challenge every skill — carpenter, smith, champion, harper, poet, physician, cupbearer, bronzeworker — and Lugh answers each with the name of the man who has it already, until he asks whether the king has one man who can do all these things; the door is opened for the Ildánach, and he hurls Ogma's flagstone back, plays sleep out of the court, and wins the throne for thirteen days.
summary.zh: 努阿達設宴塔拉，門吏逐一詰其技——木匠、鐵匠、武士、豎琴師、詩人、醫師、司酒、銅匠——魯格一一以其已有之匠名對之；直至問王有無一人兼擅百藝。門為『伊爾丹納克』（百藝之師）而開；彼擲回歐格瑪之巨石、以曲終寢滿庭、十三日得踐王座。

sensitivity.note: The polyvalence scene is the classic charter of the samildánach ('many-skilled') ideal; note that the existing base record lugh-balor overlaps this episode at the gate.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Nuada held a great feast at Teamhair, and two door-keepers were set there, for no one without an art came into Teamhair. A young man at the door said 'I am Lugh, son of Cian of the Tuatha Dé and of Ethlinn daughter of Balor.' Asked what he was skilled in, he answered 'I am a carpenter'; they had a carpenter. 'I am a smith'; they had a smith. 'I am a champion'; they had Ogma. 'I am a harper'; they had one. 'I am a poet and a teller of tales'; they had one. 'I am a magician, a physician, a cup-bearer, a worker in brass' — each was already in the king's house. Then Lugh said: 'Go and ask the king if he has any one man that can do all these things; and if he has, I will not ask to come into Teamhair.' Not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: The door-keeper told the king the young man's name should be the Ildánach, the Master of all Arts. narrative.en:
Lugh's entrance is an audition scene: the god arrives at the door of the high court and answers the gatekeeper's law — no one without an art comes into Teamhair — by out-answering it.

Nuada, restored to the kingship, held a great feast at Teamhair. Two door-keepers, Gamal son of Figal and Camel son of Riagall, stood at the gate. A young man came and bade them bring him in to the king. 'Who are you yourself?' 'I am Lugh, son of Cian of the Tuatha Dé Danann and of Ethlinn, daughter of Balor, king of the Fomor,' he said, 'foster-son of Taillte daughter of the King of the Great Plain.' 'What are you skilled in? No one without an art comes into Teamhair.'

So began the litany. 'Question me: I am a carpenter.' 'We have a carpenter, Luchtar son of Luachaid.' 'Then I am a smith.' 'We have a smith, Colum Cuaillemech of the Three New Ways.' 'I am a champion.' 'We have a champion, Ogma, brother of the king.' 'I am a harper.' 'We have a harper, Abhean son of Bicelmos.' 'I am a poet and a teller of tales.' 'We have a teller of tales, Ere son of Ethaman.' 'I am a magician.' 'We have plenty of people of power.' 'A physician.' 'We have Diancecht.' 'A cup-bearer.' 'We have nine.' 'A worker in brass.' 'We have Credne Cerd.' Each office in the pagan court was already filled — the tale inventories the whole divine civil service in one breath.

Then Lugh played his one card: 'Go and ask the king if he has any one man that can do all these things, and if he has, I will not ask to come into Teamhair.' The door-keeper brought the word in and named him: his name should be the Ildánach, the Master of all Arts. Nuada bade them try the chess-boards; every game, Lugh won. 'Let him in, for the like of him never came into Teamhair before.'

Inside, the proving continued. Ogma lifted the great flagstone that four times twenty yoke of oxen could barely move and hurled it out through the house as a challenge; Lugh hurled it back so it lay in the middle of the king's house. He took the harp and played the three strains — laughter, tears, sleep — until the court laughed, wept, and slept. Nuada, seeing that by this man's help the country might be freed from the taxes and tyranny of the Fomor, came down from his own throne and set Lugh on it for thirteen days, so that all might listen to his advice. The god of many gifts had arrived not as a warrior but as a competence — and in the war to come every specialist in the Tuatha's camp would work under his direction, exactly as the gatehouse scene promised.
narrative.zh: 魯格之入場為一場試演：神臨高廷之門，以超答之姿回應門吏之法——無藝者不得入塔拉。努阿達復位，設大宴於塔拉；門吏戈馬爾（菲加爾之子）與卡梅爾（里亞加爾之子）守門。一青年求見王：『我乃魯格，神族西安與弗摩爾王之女艾斯琳之子，大平原王之女泰爾特之養子。』問其技：『問我吧，我是木匠。』『已有木匠盧克塔爾。』『我是鐵匠。』『已有鐵匠三新道之科隆。』『我是武士。』『已有王弟歐格瑪。』『我是豎琴師。』『已有阿貝安。』『我是詩人兼講古者。』『已有埃雷。』『我是術士。』『多有其人。』『醫師。』『已有迪安徹特。』『司酒。』『已有九人。』『銅匠。』『已有克雷德·克爾德。』異教廷中百官已滿——故事一口氣盤點神族之全套文官制度。魯格遂出其絕招：『請問王：座中可有一人兼擅百藝？若有，吾不求入塔拉。』門吏入告，命名曰『伊爾丹納克』（百藝之師）。努阿達令試棋局；魯格局局皆勝。『放他進來，塔拉前所未有此人。』入門之後考驗繼續：歐格瑪舉四十八頭牛方堪移動之巨石擲出殿外為戰書；魯格擲回使其正落王殿之中。魯格執琴奏三曲——笑、哭、眠——至滿庭先笑後泣而後入睡。努阿達見此，思此人可助解弗摩爾苛政，遂自王座下而立魯格於其位十三日，使眾人聆其謀。多藝之神以「勝任」而非「勇武」入場——而後之戰中，神族營中百工皆在其調度之下，正如門前之景所許。

summary.en: The three sons of Tuireann kill Lugh's father Cian in his shape of a pig; Lugh hears it from the earth itself, and levies on them the famous fine of eight wonders — apples of the east, the healing pigskin of Greece, the spear of Persia, the sea-horses and chariot, the self-renewing pigs, the hound, the cooking-spit and three shouts on a forbidden hill — which they gather by trick, war and wound, dying on the last two items.
summary.zh: 圖雷恩三子殺魯格之父西安（時為豬形）；魯格自大地之口得知，遂課其『八件異寶』之罰——東方之蘋果、希臘愈傷豬皮、波斯之矛、海上駿馬與戰車、復生之豬、神獵犬、烹杼與禁丘三聲呼——三子以詭計、戰爭與創傷逐件得之，終死於末二項。

sensitivity.note: The eric-fine (éraic) narrative is a legal-theological myth of blood-price; symbol pin at Beinn Édair/Howth, the brothers' last view of Ireland.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Cian, traveling north alone, saw the three sons of Tuireann before him — his enemies — and struck himself with a druid rod into the shape of a pig of the herd; Brian saw through the enchantment, struck his brothers into hounds, and the pig was speared at the wood's edge. 'I was a man indeed — I am Cian, son of Cainte; give me your protection.' 'If the life came back seven times to you, I would take it from you every time.' Cian won one request — to die in his own shape, 'for then the blood-fine will be heavier than ever was paid' — and they pelted him with stones till only a broken heap was left; the earth cast up their burial six times, and kept it on the seventh. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book Two ch. 2; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: The earth spoke to Lugh: 'in great danger your father was here, and into the shape of a pig he had to go, but in his own shape they killed him.' At Teamhair Lugh asked the assembly what vengeance each would take on his father's killer; all said day-by-day mutilation — 'and there are making that answer the three men that killed my father.' Brian, thinking to keep the fine small, offered to pay; Lugh named three apples from the Garden in the East of the World, the pigskin of Tuis king of Greece that heals all wounds, the deadly spear of the king of Persia, the sea-running horses and chariot of Siogair, the seven pigs of Easal killed each night and alive next morning, the whelp Fail-Inis before whom all wild beasts fall, a cooking-spit of the women of the Island of Fair-Hair, and three shouts on the hill of Miochaoin. The fine was bound under guarantees; a druid spell of forgetfulness later robbed them of the last two items. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book Two ch. 2; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: As hawks they took the apples under a storm of spears; the king's three daughters, as ospreys, scorched them with lightning, and Brian turned them into swans. As poets they won and stole the pigskin and slew Tuis; they killed the king of Persia with one of the apples to win the spear; as hired soldiers they seized the chariot and horses. Easal, king of the Golden Pillars, gave the pigs freely — the only item won without fighting — and helped win the hound at Ioruaidh. A year quartered on the sea bought the cooking-spit from the laughing women. At the hill of Miochaoin they were speared through the body; Brian raised each dying brother with one hand till the three shouts were given, and Tuireann's plea for the healing skin was refused — 'unless I were sure your death would come on you.' Brian lay down between his brothers, and the three lives went out together. Not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The tale of the Sons of Tuireann is the Irish saga of a fine — the eric (éraic) — carried to world's end, and Ireland's most sustained study of how vengeance becomes commerce.

The sons of Tuireann — Brian, Iuchar and Iucharba, the best of Teamhair for skill and name — had hatred between their line and the three sons of Cainte. Meeting Cian alone on the Plain of Muirthemne, they caught him changing shape: he struck himself with a druid rod into a pig of the herd. Brian alone understood the enchantment, turned his brothers into hounds, and speared the pig at the wood's edge. 'It is a bad thing you have done, to make a cast at me when you knew me.' Asked for protection, Brian swore he would take the life seven times over. Cian won a single request: to die in his own shape — 'for if you had killed me in the shape of a pig there would be only the blood-money of a pig on me; but in my own shape there never was, and never will be, any person killed for whose sake a heavier fine will be paid than for myself. And the arms I am killed with, it is they will tell the deed to my son.' They stoned him to a broken heap; the earth refused the burial six times and took it on the seventh.

Lugh heard the tale from the earth itself, and buried his father with an ogham stone. At Teamhair he shook the chain of silence and asked the assembly what vengeance they would take on their father's killer: day-by-day mutilation until the end — 'and there are making that answer the three men that killed my father.' Trickery followed: to keep the fine small, Brian answered 'we will pay the fine as if we did kill him.' Lugh then named the eight items with false modesty — three apples from the Garden in the East of the World, golden as burned gold, tasting of honey, that take away wound-pain and sickness and never lessen; the pigskin of Tuis of Greece that heals all wounds and turns streams to wine; the spear of the king of Persia, its head kept under water lest it burn the place; the horses of Dobar that run on sea as on land and their matchless chariot; the seven pigs of Easal, killed every night, found alive at morning, that keep eaters free of sickness; the whelp Fail-Inis before which all the wild beasts of the world fall down; a cooking-spit from the women of Inis Cenn-fhinne; and three shouts on the hill of Miochaoin — where Miochaoin and his sons were under bonds to allow no shout, for they held Lugh's father's learning, and would never forgive.

The gathering of the fine is an odyssey of disguise: hawks under the spears of the garden-guardians, turned to swans by Brian's rod to escape the lightning of the king's three osprey-daughters; poets who win the pigskin of Tuis with a riddling poem and murder the court; a cast of the apple that kills the king of Persia; hired soldiers who seize the chariot at a fair. Only Easal, king of the Golden Pillars, gives freely — the pigs — and then helps at Ioruaidh for the hound, trading battle for peace. A druid spell of forgetfulness, sent by Lugh, makes the brothers come home thinking all is paid; the missing spit and shouts are named publicly, and Tuireann's daughter Ethne laments them back to the sea. A quarter of a year on the ocean wins the spit from the laughing embroiderers. Then the hill of Miochaoin: guardian and sons, mutual spearing, Brian lifting each dying brother with one hand until the three shouts were given at last. Tuireann begged the healing skin of Lugh — 'for we are of the one blood, and let him not give hardness for hardness.' Lugh refused: not for the breadth of the earth in gold, unless he was sure their death would come in satisfaction for the deed. Brian lay down between his brothers, and the three lives went out together; their father died of grief and they were buried in one grave.
narrative.zh: 圖雷恩諸子之故事乃愛爾蘭之『罰金史詩』（éraic），將復仇化為商業之最持久研究。圖雷恩三子——布萊恩、尤哈、尤哈爾巴——技藝與名望冠絕塔拉，與西安三兄弟世代為仇。穆爾西姆尼平原上孤身之西安被擒，以德魯伊杖化為豬形；惟布萊恩識破，化二弟為獵犬，林緣一矛刺中。『知我而射，惡莫大焉。』求庇不得；布萊恩誓取其命七次。西安求得一事：死於人形——『若以豬形殺我，賠償僅如一豬之價；以人形殺我，則世上從無、永無為其人賠償更重之罰金。且所用之器，將向吾子訴此事。』石擊至碎；地六次拒納其屍，第七次乃受。魯格自大地親聞其事，葬父立石、刻歐甘文。於塔拉搖靜默之鏈，問眾人：殺父者當受何報？眾曰日日肢解——『而作此答者，正是殺我父之三子。』布萊恩欲以小額罰金了事，答『如我所殺亦當賠』。魯格遂以假謙列八件：東方世界花園之蘋果三枚（金如鎔金、味如蜜、除創痛與病、永不減少）；希臘王圖伊斯之豬皮（愈百創、化水為酒）；波斯王之矛（矛首浸水以防其焚其所）；西奧蓋爾王之海行雙馬與無雙戰車；埃薩爾王之七豬（夜殺晨生、食者無疾）；伊俄魯伊之犬費爾-伊尼斯（百獸見之皆伏）；妙髮之島婦之烹杼一支；米奧肯禁丘之三聲呼（守丘者與其子誓不許呼，因魯格之父之學藝在其處，永不寬恕）。取寶之旅即偽裝之旅：以鷹形入花園避矛雨、為避王之三魚鷹女之雷電化為天鵝；以詩人形得豬皮而屠其廷；擲蘋果殺波斯王；以傭兵形於市集奪車馬。惟埃薩爾王甘願獻豬——八寶中惟一不戰而得者——繼而助於伊俄魯伊以戰易和取犬。魯格復遣遺忘之咒，使三子誤以為罰已畢；缺失之杼與三呼於眾前點明，圖雷恩之女埃特尼泣別於海。四月之航自繡女之笑聲中得杼。禁丘之上，守者與三子互矛貫體；布萊恩以一手扶起垂死之弟，直到三聲呼畢。圖雷恩求魯格賜愈皮——『我們血脈相連，勿以硬報硬』——魯格拒之：縱以大地之廣之金易之亦不與，除非確信其死足以償其罪。布萊恩臥於二弟之間，三命同盡；父悲而亡，同穴而葬。

Etiology of the treasures: Lugh's spear, the sword Fragarach and other war-gear enter the Tuatha's arsenal by this fine

summary.en: The sons of Miled sail from the south to avenge Ith, their kinsman slain at Tara; Amergin stakes the landing on nine waves against the druid winds, five sons drown, and on the quieted shore Amergin speaks the great 'I am' poem — wind, wave, bull, eagle, salmon — before the Gael and the Tuatha Dé settle the island in battle at Tailltiu.
summary.zh: 米勒德諸子為報伊特之仇自南方揚帆；阿莫金以九浪之約與德魯伊風暴相賭，五子溺亡；風浪既平，阿莫金於岸誦『我是』之詩——風、浪、牛、鷹、鮭——蓋爾人與達娜之民遂決戰於塔爾提烏而定島屬。

sensitivity.note: The Milesian conquest is the charter myth of Gaelic Ireland; collected from public-domain print. The landing-place Inver Sceine is identified with Bantry Bay in tradition.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: The druids of the sons of Miled told them there was no country for them to settle in till they came to the island in the west — 'and if you do not get possession of it yourselves, your children will get possession of it.' The Tuatha Dé cast a cloud of enchantment over the island so the fleet saw only a pig-like shape; they rounded the coast and landed at Inver Sceine. On the way to Teamhair they met three queens of the Sídhe one after another — Banba wife of Mac Cuill son of the Hazel, Fodhla wife of Mac Cecht son of the Plough, and Eriu wife of Mac Greine son of the Sun, who was in one moment a wide-eyed beautiful queen and in another a sharp-beaked grey-white crow — and each queen's name would afterward be a name of Ireland. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book Three ch. 1; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Amergin offered the Tuatha Dé the wager: he would draw his ships out the length of nine waves from the shore; if the Men of Dea could keep them from landing he would sail away for ever, but if the Sons of the Gael landed, the Tuatha Dé should give up the kingship. The Men of Dea raised a druid wind that scattered the fleet and drowned Donn with twenty-four of his people, and Ir, and Colpa of the Sword — five of the sons of Miled destroyed. Donn called it treachery, and Amergin said his incantation over the sea: 'that they that are tossing in the great wide food-giving sea may reach now to the land... let our chief men, let their learned wives, ask that we may come to the noble woman, great Eriu.' The wind went down, and Amergin, first on the shore, said: 'I am the wind on the sea; I am the wave of the sea; I am the bull of seven battles; I am the eagle on the rock; I am a flash from the sun; I am the most beautiful of plants; I am a strong wild boar; I am a salmon in the water; I am a lake in the plain; I am the word of knowledge; I am the head of the spear in battle; I am the god that puts fire in the head.' Not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The last invasion of Ireland is a lawsuit settled at sea, and its hero is a poet whose only weapon is grammar.

The sons of Miled — the Milesians, the Gael — came from the south under the leadership of the sons of Miled, their druids having told them there was no country for them to settle in until they came to the island in the west: 'and if you do not get possession of it yourselves, your children will get possession of it.' They sailed first to avenge Ith, their kinsman, who had come to the Tuatha's court in an earlier generation and been killed there by treachery. The Men of Dea did not wait for negotiation: they cast such a cloud of enchantment over the island that the fleet could see only a large thing shaped like a pig, and the Gael were hindered from landing until they worked round the coast to Inver Sceine in the west of Munster.

Marching inland, they met the land itself three times. At Slieve Mis a queen with her women and druids came out and gave her name: Banba, wife of Mac Cuill, Son of the Hazel. At Slieve Eibhline: Fodhla, wife of Mac Cecht, Son of the Plough. At Uisnech a woman met them who was in one moment a wide-eyed most beautiful queen, and in another a sharp-beaked, grey-white crow — Eriu, wife of Mac Greine, Son of the Sun. The island kept three names because it had three claimants; in the aftertime the poets would call Ireland by all of them.

At Teamhair the three grandsons of the Dagda held the kingship between them, quarrelling over their father's treasures. Amergin put the case to them and proposed the wager: let the Gael go out the length of nine waves from shore; if the Men of Dea can keep them from landing, the Gael will sail away for ever — but if they land, the Tuatha Dé give up the kingship. The gods took the enchantment side. They raised a druid wind that scattered the fleet and broke the ship of Donn, who was drowned with four-and-twenty men and women; Ir died in the same storm, and Colpa of the Sword at the moment of landing: five of the sons of Miled destroyed by weather.

Donn, before the sea took him, called it treachery, 'our knowledgeable men not putting down this wind.' Amergin answered there was no treachery — and rose before the ships and made his incantation over the winds and the sea: that they that are tossing in the great wide food-giving sea may reach now to the land; that they may find a place upon its plains, its mountains, and its valleys; that there may be a king of their own in Teamhair; that their chief men and their learned wives may ask that they come to the noble woman, great Eriu. The wind went down. Amergin stepped first onto the shore and said the great poem: I am the wind on the sea; I am the wave of the sea; I am the bull of seven battles; I am the eagle on the rock; I am a flash from the sun; I am the most beautiful of plants; I am a strong wild boar; I am a salmon in the water; I am a lake in the plain; I am the word of knowledge; I am the head of the spear in battle; I am the god that puts fire in the head. Who spreads light in the gathering on the hills? Who can tell the ages of the moon? Who can tell the place where the sun rests?

Three days later the first battle was fought at Sliab Mis, where Scota, wife of Miled, fell; the decisive battle of Tailltiu killed the three kings and three queens of the Tuatha Dé, and the surviving gods went under the hills. The poets' settlement of the defeat endures in one sentence: every brave fighting man was of the Sons of the Gael; every skilled man of music and secret enchantment was of the Tuatha Dé Danann — the two peoples of Ireland, army and dream, ranked and named.
narrative.zh: 愛爾蘭最後一次入侵，是一場以詩句為武器、在海上結案之訴訟。米勒德諸子（即蓋爾人）自南方而來，其德魯伊曾告：無他處可居，必至西方之島——『若爾等自不能得之，爾之子孫將得之。』彼等首先為族人伊特復仇——伊特昔年至達娜之民之廷而被謀害。神族不待談判：以咒雲蔽島，使艦隊惟見一豬形巨物；蓋爾人繞岸而至芒斯特西部因弗·斯凱恩登陸。內進途中，三次與土地相會：斯利夫·米斯山遇女王班巴（榛子之子麥克·庫爾之妻）；斯利夫·艾夫林遇福德拉（犁之子麥克·克赫特之妻）；烏斯內克遇一女，頃刻為美目之後，頃刻為灰白銳喙之鴉——艾雷（太陽之子麥克·格賴內之妻）。島有三名，因其有三主；後世詩人遂以三名稱愛爾蘭。塔拉城中，達格達三孫共治而爭產。阿莫金陳案立約：蓋爾人退出九浪之外；若神族能阻其登岸，則永不再來；若登岸，神族讓位。神族以德魯伊風暴應之：艦隊潰散，唐恩與二十四人溺亡，伊爾死於同風暴，劍之科爾帕死於將登之際——米勒德五子皆喪於天氣。唐恩臨沒斥為背信；阿莫金答曰無信——起於舟前向風海誦咒：使飄搖於廣闊賜食之海者今得登陸；使彼等得處其平原、山嶽、溪谷；使塔拉有吾族之王；使吾人之首領與智婦求見偉大之艾雷。風止。阿莫金率先登岸，誦其大詩：我是海上之風；我是海中之浪；我是七戰之牛；我是岩上之鷹；我是日中之一閃；我是至美之草；我是荒野之豬；我是水中之鮭；我是平原之湖；我是知識之言；我是戰中之矛鋒；我是點燃頭腦之火之神。孰於山丘聚會中散布光明？孰能言月亮之齡？孰能言太陽安息之所？三日後斯利夫·米斯首戰，米勒德之妻斯科塔陣亡；塔爾提烏決戰殺神族三王三后，倖存之神入山而居。詩人對敗者之安置存於一句：凡勇戰之士屬蓋爾人之子；凡精於音樂與隱秘咒法者屬達娜之民——愛爾蘭之二族，軍隊與夢，各得其位、各得其名。

functions: Founding charter of Gaelic Ireland: conquest legitimized as a won wager and a paid blood-debt for Ith
Charter of the poet's authority: Amergin's poem as grammar of national identity ('I am' catalog)
Etiology of Ireland's three names (Banba, Fodla, Eriu) from the three queens met on the march
Settlement of the two peoples: fighters of the Gael, craft-and-enchantment people of the Tuatha Dé

variants.text_tradition: Book of Leinster and later MSS
variants.summary: The chronicle gives full genealogies of the Milesians from Scota and Goídel Glas and a set of Amergin's invocations (to land, sea, fish) before the landing — the liturgical core of the conquest.

variants.name: Folk remains of Donn
variants.text_tradition: Dindsenchas and later folklore of Tech Duinn
variants.summary: Donn the drowned son becomes lord of the dead: 'to me, to my house, you shall all come after your deaths' — his shipwreck is the mythic origin of the Irish house of the dead.
